summary: A 1970 note on the aftermath of a network meeting, with an epilogue and miscellaneous items. It records outcomes and follow-up points rather than defining a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This 1970 note is the minutes-plus-follow-up of a network design meeting at UCLA. It reports that a new protocol built on sockets was broadly accepted, collects later suggestions about reconnection, defines what the group means by a process, and lists mailing list changes.

questions: what was discussed at the march 1970 network meeting
what is a process in networking
why are sockets important in early network protocol
subtitle: Notes from an early network protocol design meeting in 1970.

tldr.problem: Early ARPANET developers needed to coordinate on protocol design and share feedback after meetings.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 37 documents a March 1970 network meeting discussing protocol modifications including dynamic reconnection, and records follow-up conversations.
tldr.outcome: This artifact captures the early design discussions that shaped network protocol development, including debates about sockets, connections, and links.

today: The unit metadata records the status of RFC 37 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a historical record of early ARPANET protocol discussions that shaped socket-based network communication.

sections.title: Meeting Record
sections.content:
On March 17, 1970, Steve Crocker hosted a network meeting at UCLA with about 25 people from sites across the ARPANET, including MIT, LL, BBN, Harvard, SRI, Utah, UCSB, SDC, RAND and UCLA. Crocker presented a modification of the protocol in RFC 33, sketchily documented in RFC 36, whose main change was a facility for dynamic reconnection.

The protocol based on sockets and undistinguished simplex connections differed greatly from the earlier one in RFC 11. The push for change came from a December 1969 meeting at Utah, where the limits of a log-in requirement and the inability to connect arbitrary processes were challenged.
sections.plainLanguage: Computer scientists from many places met to hear about a new way for programs to connect without a log-in step, and to say what they thought of it.

sections.title: The Protocol Debate
sections.content:
Crocker judged that the protocol was widely accepted, with criticism falling into two groups: doubts about the complexity and usefulness of the full protocol, especially dynamic reconnection, and other topics such as character set translation, higher level languages and incompatible equipment. Notably lacking was criticism of the basic ideas of sockets and connections.

The group agreed that Crocker would publish an implementable specification by April 30, that anyone wanting changes would say so at once, that a further meeting would follow any major modification, and that Jim Forgie of Lincoln Labs would tentatively host a meeting on higher level network languages.

Afterwards, Bill Crowther of BBN sent two ideas: an exchange of I want to reconnect messages between neighbors, and a proposal to decouple connections from links so any handy link could carry a connection's messages, putting source and destination socket numbers in the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: People argued about how hard the new scheme should be and whether a connection and the actual communication line should be separate ideas. Crocker promised a finished specification by the end of April.

sections.title: Process, Sockets and Room to Grow
sections.content:
RFC 37 defines process to mean a program with an assigned location counter and an address space, as against a program, which is merely a pattern of bits stored in a file. A new process is created only by an existing process, and a process may end itself or be ended by another. Because two processes can be externally indistinguishable, Crocker argued that sockets are needed as a standard interface between them.

RAND's John Heafner and Erick Harslem pointed out that the protocol had no provision for error detection and reporting, status testing, or expansion and experimentation. Crocker proposed reserving room by using only the first 32 of the 256 links and by assigning permanent command codes from 255 downward.
sections.plainLanguage: A process is a running program with its own memory and identity. Sockets are a shared meeting point that lets one process find another. The group also agreed to leave spare numbers free for future growth.
